title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 4: The Reaction Log
description: Four separate incidents in one morning — a rusted sign, a decomposed sample, a discolored coin, and a cloudy test tube. Every entry in the reaction log needs a balanced equation and a correct classification.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Treats every incident report as a chance to test your reasoning.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Wants to write 'chemical stuff happened' and call it a day.

reaction_types_chart.name: Reaction Types Chart
reaction_types_chart.description: Synthesis, decomposition, single/double displacement, side by side.

activity_series.name: Activity Series Card
activity_series.description: Ranks metals from most to least reactive.

elements.text: Four incidents this morning, four log entries needed — each one needs a balanced equation and the right reaction type before it's filed.
Can I just write 'a reaction occurred' for all four?

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the reaction types chart.

options.text: "No — balance each equation and classify the reaction type properly."

elements.text: First, evidence: color change, gas production, a precipitate forming, or a temperature change all suggest a chemical reaction happened. A shape change alone does not — that's physical, not chemical.
Second, every equation has to balance — same number of each atom on both sides, adjusted only by coefficients, never by changing subscripts.

config.question: Which observation is NOT, by itself, evidence that a chemical reaction occurred?

options.text: Gas bubbles forming in the solution
A sample changing shape when it's crushed into powder

config.explanation: Crushing a solid changes its shape and surface area, but it's still the same substance — a physical change, not chemical evidence.

config.prompt: The rusted sign: Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3 is unbalanced. The fully balanced form is 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3. What coefficient goes in front of Fe?

elements.text: Synthesis: two or more substances combine into one, A + B -> AB. The rusted sign is synthesis — iron and oxygen combining into iron oxide. Decomposition is the reverse: one substance breaks apart into two or more, AB -> A + B.

config.prompt: Sort each equation by reaction type.

elements.text: One entry says a coin came out of a copper sulfate solution looking different — zinc-plated, almost. What happened there?

Single displacement: a more reactive element pushes a less reactive one out of a compound, A + BC -> AC + B. The activity series ranks metals by reactivity — a metal can only displace something below it on the list.

config.question: Zinc metal is dropped into a copper(II) sulfate solution: Zn + CuSO4 -> ? (zinc is more reactive than copper)

options.text: ZnSO4 + Cu — zinc displaces copper from the compound
ZnCu + SO4, a combined metal compound

config.explanation: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the sulfate compound, forming zinc sulfate and depositing solid copper.

config.prompt: Copper is less reactive than zinc. If copper metal is added to a zinc sulfate solution (Cu + ZnSO4), does a displacement reaction occur? Answer yes or no.

elements.text: The cloudy test tube is double displacement: two compounds swap partners, AB + CD -> AD + CB. It's usually driven forward by a precipitate, a gas, or water forming — something that pulls the reaction out of the original mixture.

config.prompt: Silver nitrate solution is mixed with sodium chloride solution: AgNO3 + NaCl -> ? Give the two products, separated by a plus sign, no spaces (e.g. AgCl+NaNO3).

config.question: In a double displacement reaction, what typically drives the reaction forward — real evidence it actually happened?

options.text: Formation of a precipitate, a gas, or water
An increase in total mass of the system
Both reactants must be gases to begin with
The reaction must be heated above 100 degrees C

config.explanation: A precipitate, gas, or water forming removes ions from solution, pulling the reaction toward products.

elements.text: Synthesis, decomposition, single displacement, double displacement — every entry balanced and classified. That's a real log.
It's filed, but a couple of entries needed a second pass. Let's tighten up the classification rules next time.

elements.prompt: The log is ready to submit. What now?

options.text: Show Dev how the reactant/product pattern predicts the reaction type every time, using all four entries.
File it and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So it's never a guess — count the reactants and products, check the activity series if a metal's involved, and the type falls out of the pattern.

ending.title: Reaction Classifier
ending.description: Balanced and classified all four incidents correctly, and taught Dev the underlying pattern.

ending.title: Log Filed
ending.description: All four incidents are logged. The deeper classification pattern can wait.
